-- Converted: CREATE JOIN INDEX sales.jix_order -> CREATE VIEW SALES.JIX_ORDER with the same projection and inner join
-- Reason: Snowflake materialized views cannot contain joins and has no join indexes; a view keeps the exact row set (inner join, duplicates kept, NULL ORDER_ID rows excluded) and is always consistent with the base tables, as the join index was. Plain CREATE (no OR REPLACE) keeps the error if the object already exists.
-- Converted: implicit join JOIN -> explicit INNER JOIN; table aliases and columns uppercased and fully qualified via the naming map
-- Reason: Same semantics, explicit join type for readability.
CREATE VIEW SALES.JIX_ORDER (ORDER_ID, PRODUCT_ID) AS
SELECT
    h.ORDER_ID,
    l.PRODUCT_ID
FROM SALES.ORDER_HEADER h
INNER JOIN SALES.ORDER_LINE l
    ON h.ORDER_ID = l.ORDER_ID;

The client connection uses key-pair authentication and has USAGE on SALES and SELECT on SALES.CUSTOMER.
Result size is below the 5 GB single-file limit (MAX_FILE_SIZE set just under it).
@~/migraai_export/customer.csv is the user stage (a file location), not a table; static checkers that treat it as a table reference report a false positive.

Client-only BTEQ commands (.LOGON, .SET QUIET, .EXPORT RESET, .LOGOFF) mapped to connection/client options.
The naming-map target "ZIP/LOAD_SCRIPT".SQL names the source file, not a database object, so no object is created.

files.content:
-- Converted: .LOGON (masked credentials) -> removed; connect with a SnowSQL / Snowflake CLI named connection (e.g. snow sql -c <connection> -f load_script.sql)
-- Reason: Credentials must not be embedded in scripts; the connection should use key-pair authentication configured outside the script.
-- Converted: .SET QUIET ON -> removed; use client option quiet (snowsql -o quiet=true -o friendly=false)
-- Reason: Output verbosity is a client setting, not SQL.
-- Converted: .EXPORT FILE = /tmp/customer.csv + SEL ... -> COPY INTO the user stage as one uncompressed CSV file
-- Reason: Snowflake exports query results server-side with COPY INTO <location>; SEL is the Teradata abbreviation of SELECT. Columns stay explicit; no ORDER BY is added because the source had none (row order is unspecified in both systems).
COPY INTO @~/migraai_export/customer.csv
FROM (
    SELECT
        c.CUSTOMER_ID,
        c.CUSTOMER_NAME
    FROM SALES.CUSTOMER c
)
FILE_FORMAT = (
    TYPE = CSV
    FIELD_DELIMITER = ','
    FIELD_OPTIONALLY_ENCLOSED_BY = '"'
    NULL_IF = ('')
    EMPTY_FIELD_AS_NULL = FALSE
    COMPRESSION = NONE
)
HEADER = TRUE
SINGLE = TRUE
OVERWRITE = TRUE
MAX_FILE_SIZE = 4900000000;

-- Converted: export target /tmp/customer.csv -> GET the staged file to the client directory /tmp/
-- Reason: COPY INTO writes to a stage; GET downloads it to the machine running the client, matching the client-side file written by BTEQ.
GET @~/migraai_export/customer.csv file:///tmp/;

-- Converted: .EXPORT RESET -> remove the staged copy
-- Reason: Ends the export and avoids leaving data in the user stage.
REMOVE @~/migraai_export/customer.csv;

-- Converted: .LOGOFF -> removed
-- Reason: The client session ends when the script finishes.

unsupported: Exact BTEQ export file layout: the default BTEQ .EXPORT format (record/REPORT mode, fixed-width columns, '?' for NULL, column titles) cannot be reproduced by COPY INTO; downstream consumers of /tmp/customer.csv must accept standard CSV.

assumptions: Teradata session (BTET) mode with the CALL issued outside an explicit transaction: each statement commits on its own, which matches Snowflake procedures running with AUTOCOMMIT on. If a caller wraps the CALL in an explicit transaction, rollback behaviour must be reviewed.
Target tables already exist (earlier objects in this batch / earlier batches) with the columns in the dependency signatures.
Session database is set so SALES.<object> resolves.
RETURNS VARCHAR with RETURN NULL stands in for a Teradata procedure that returns no value; callers ignore the return value.

SALES.AUDIT_LOG is a Teradata SET table (created as SET in this batch), so inserting an identical row raises error 2802; this is emulated with a pre-insert check that raises -20802. The check uses exact comparison, while Teradata NOT CASESPECIFIC columns would also treat case/trailing-blank variants as duplicates.

SALES.PAYMENT is not defined in this batch, so its SET/MULTISET kind is unknown; no duplicate check was added for it. If it was a SET table, a repeated (1, p_account, p_amount) row would have failed in Teradata but succeeds here.
Decimal rounding when a caller passes more than 2 decimals: Snowflake rounds half away from zero on the cast to NUMBER(12,2); Teradata's rounding mode depends on the RoundHalfwayMagUp setting.
explanations: Converted to a Snowflake Scripting procedure with EXECUTE AS OWNER (from SQL SECURITY OWNER).

-- Converted: CREATE PROCEDURE sales.add_payment(IN p_account BIGINT, IN p_amount DECIMAL(12, 2)) -> CREATE PROCEDURE SALES.ADD_PAYMENT(P_ACCOUNT NUMBER(19,0), P_AMOUNT NUMBER(12,2)) RETURNS VARCHAR LANGUAGE SQL
-- Reason: Snowflake Scripting procedure; IN is the only parameter mode, BIGINT/DECIMAL mapped to exact NUMBER types; Snowflake requires a RETURNS clause, so RETURN NULL stands in for no return value. Plain CREATE keeps the error if it already exists.
-- Converted: SQL SECURITY OWNER -> EXECUTE AS OWNER
-- Reason: Both run the body with the owner's privileges.
-- Converted: DYNAMIC RESULT SETS 1 -> removed
-- Reason: The body never opens a result-set cursor, so the procedure returns no result set in either system.
CREATE PROCEDURE SALES.ADD_PAYMENT(P_ACCOUNT NUMBER(19,0), P_AMOUNT NUMBER(12,2))
RETURNS VARCHAR
LANGUAGE SQL
EXECUTE AS OWNER
AS
$$
DECLARE
    dup_count NUMBER(38,0) DEFAULT 0;
    duplicate_row EXCEPTION (-20802, 'Duplicate row in SET table SALES.AUDIT_LOG (EVENT_ID 1, EVENT_TYPE PAYMENT)');
BEGIN
    -- Converted: INSERT INTO sales.payment ... VALUES (1, p_account, p_amount) -> same insert with bind variables and explicit casts
    -- Reason: Parameters are referenced as :NAME in Snowflake Scripting SQL; explicit casts keep the source types.
    INSERT INTO SALES.PAYMENT (PAYMENT_ID, ACCOUNT_ID, AMOUNT)
    VALUES (CAST(1 AS NUMBER(19,0)), CAST(:P_ACCOUNT AS NUMBER(19,0)), CAST(:P_AMOUNT AS NUMBER(12,2)));

    -- Converted: SET-table duplicate-row error on SALES.AUDIT_LOG -> explicit existence check that raises -20802
    -- Reason: SALES.AUDIT_LOG was a Teradata SET table; inserting an identical row failed with error 2802 after the payment row had already been committed. Snowflake would silently accept the duplicate.
    SELECT COUNT(*) INTO :dup_count
    FROM SALES.AUDIT_LOG t
    WHERE t.EVENT_ID = 1
      AND t.EVENT_TYPE = 'PAYMENT';
    IF (dup_count > 0) THEN
        RAISE duplicate_row;
    END IF;

    -- Converted: INSERT INTO sales.audit_log ... VALUES (1, 'PAYMENT') -> same insert with explicit casts
    -- Reason: Keeps the column types of SALES.AUDIT_LOG.
    INSERT INTO SALES.AUDIT_LOG (EVENT_ID, EVENT_TYPE)
    VALUES (CAST(1 AS NUMBER(19,0)), CAST('PAYMENT' AS VARCHAR(40)));

    RETURN NULL;
END;
$$;

RETURNS VARCHAR
LANGUAGE SQL
EXECUTE AS OWNER
AS

END;
$$;

-- Converted: CREATE PROCEDURE sales.capture_snapshot() -> CREATE PROCEDURE SALES.CAPTURE_SNAPSHOT() RETURNS VARCHAR LANGUAGE SQL
-- Reason: Snowflake Scripting procedure; RETURNS is mandatory, so RETURN NULL stands in for no return value. Plain CREATE keeps the error if it already exists.
-- Converted: default SQL SECURITY (DEFINER) -> EXECUTE AS OWNER
-- Reason: Closest Snowflake equivalent of definer's rights; Snowflake requires the clause to be explicit.
CREATE PROCEDURE SALES.CAPTURE_SNAPSHOT()
RETURNS VARCHAR
LANGUAGE SQL
EXECUTE AS OWNER
AS
$$
BEGIN
    -- Converted: INSERT ... SELECT CURRENT_DATE, account_id FROM sales.account -> INSERT ... SELECT CURRENT_DATE(), ACCOUNT_ID FROM SALES."ACCOUNT" MINUS existing SALES.ACCOUNT_SNAPSHOT rows
    -- Reason: SALES.ACCOUNT_SNAPSHOT was a Teradata SET table, and INSERT...SELECT in Teradata mode silently discards rows that duplicate each other or existing rows (NULLs compare equal). MINUS gives exactly that: distinct rows, NULL-safe, minus rows already present. CURRENT_DATE() is evaluated once per statement in both systems.
    INSERT INTO SALES.ACCOUNT_SNAPSHOT (SNAPSHOT_DATE, ACCOUNT_ID)
    SELECT
        CURRENT_DATE(),
        CAST(a.ACCOUNT_ID AS NUMBER(19,0))
    FROM SALES."ACCOUNT" a
    MINUS
    SELECT
        s.SNAPSHOT_DATE,
        s.ACCOUNT_ID
    FROM SALES.ACCOUNT_SNAPSHOT s;

    RETURN NULL;
END;
$$;
